top.label: Banks
top.blurb: Deposits, loans, and payments. Sized by balance sheet — what a bank holds, not what it manages for someone else.

sub.label: Sparkassen
sub.blurb: Public savings banks. Each city or county owns one. Retail deposits and local lending are the core business. 342 exist nationally; our data covers a fraction of them.

sub.label: Landesbanken
sub.blurb: Wholesale banks owned by state governments and regional Sparkassen groups. They fund Sparkassen, lend to state-linked projects, and run capital-markets desks. Only 6 exist.

institutions.parent: DZ BANK AG Deutsche Zentral-Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt am Main
detail_lines: Parent: DZ BANK AG Deutsche Zentral-Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt am Main.

sub.label: Förderbanken
sub.blurb: State-owned development banks. KfW is the largest. They fund policy goals — housing, exports, small business, green energy — rather than compete for retail deposits.

detail_lines: Thüringer Aufbaubank -Anstalt des öffentlichen Rechts- — €3.6bn assets (2025).

sub.label: Großbanken
sub.blurb: The three national full-service banks. Retail, corporate, and investment banking under one roof, nationwide branch networks.

sub.label: Regionalbanken
sub.blurb: Everyone else with a German banking license: foreign banks' German subsidiaries, auto-finance banks, direct banks, and smaller private banks. A wide mix of sizes and models.

detail_lines: Parent: J.P. Morgan International Finance Limited.
Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE — €107.2bn assets (2024).
State Street Bank International GmbH — €49.5bn assets (2025).
Citigroup Global Markets Europe AG — €41.9bn assets (2024).

sub.label: Realkreditinstitute
sub.blurb: Mortgage banks. They fund long-term property loans, often through covered bonds (Pfandbriefe). A small, specialized group.

sub.label: Bausparkassen
sub.blurb: Building societies. Customers save into a contract for years, then get a cheap home loan. A specific, regulated product line, not a general bank.

detail_lines: Parent: DZ BANK AG Deutsche Zentral-Genossenschaftsbank, Frankfurt am Main.

top.label: Asset Managers
top.blurb: They invest money on behalf of clients. The money stays the client's. Sized by assets under management, not by the manager's own balance sheet.

sub.label: Bank- and insurer-owned managers
sub.blurb: Fund managers owned by a bank or insurer group, such as DWS (Deutsche Bank). Most German fund money sits here.

sub.label: Independent managers
sub.blurb: Fund managers not owned by a bank or insurer — founder-owned or independently listed firms. Fewer of them, and smaller in total AUM than the bank-owned group.

top.label: Insurers
top.blurb: They collect premiums and pay claims. Sized by capital investments (Kapitalanlagen) — the closest public sector figure available. No official total-assets figure exists.

sub.label: Reinsurers
sub.blurb: Insurers of insurers. Munich Re and Hannover Re write policies for other insurance companies, not individuals or businesses. Germany is home to two of the world's largest.

sub.label: Primary insurers
sub.blurb: Life, health, and property/casualty insurers that sell directly to individuals and businesses. The bulk of the German insurance industry by company count.
